abstract:
Research on Generative AI (GenAI) and work reports both productivity-compressing and inequality-expanding effects, leaving open a central question for organizations: Who benefits from GenAI and on which specific tasks? I address this question through a randomized controlled trial in competitive university debating, where participants are randomly assigned access to GenAI. Although most previous experimental work examines the impact of GenAI on written activities and across individuals, this setting allows me to study the impact of GenAI on a knowledge-intensive spoken activity and to identify heterogeneous effects across subtasks. I find that GenAI expands performance inequality in this setting. Consistent with recent theories on GenAI and work, results show that high-ability participants experience significantly larger gains from GenAI usage than their lower-ability counterparts in judgment-intensive subtasks, whereas lower-ability individuals only improve their performance in less expert components of debating, where GenAI can be used as a substitute. If these inequality-expanding effects generalize to similar spoken settings where complex ideas must be internalized and explained, rather than simply written, they would have important implications for understanding the impact of GenAI on work and inequality.
                  This paper was accepted by Maria Guadalupe, business strategy.
                  Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2025.01063 .

title: When GenAI Increases Inequality: Evidence from a University Debating Competition
